Scenes of domestic violence in films 
†*261.  SHRIMATI CHANDRA KALA PANDEY:†† 
SHRIMATI SAROJ DUBEY: 
Will the Minister of INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Film Censor Board is empowered to censor the scenes 
promoting domestic violence in the films; 
(b) if so, whether the Board is discharging its duties in an appropriate 
manner; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF INFORMATION 
AND BROADCASTING (SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD): (a) to (c) A 
Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC) certifies films in 
terms of the provisions of the Cinematograph Act, 1952 and the guidelines issued 
thereunder. These guidelines, inter alia, as CBFC to ensure that: 
(a) dhowing  involvement of children in violence as victims or as 
perpetrators or as forced witness to violence, or showing children as 
being subjected to any form of child abuse are not presented 
needlessly;

problem of less production in cement existed. As I mentioned, there was 
reduction in the supply of cement only in one year, about two years ago. Barring 
that, in each year, the capacities have increased, and during the Tenth Plan 
period there is a further increase of capacities that is anticipated. A bulk of the 
cement production is in the private sector and there is a lot of competition 
today in the private sector, and it is that competition which is really holding 
the price line. Now, with regard to prices varying from State to States. The 
price variation depends upon the distance that the product has to cover to

other States, particularly in the Nort-East and Jammu and Kashmir where 
distances are large; and in addition to distances, on account of local taxation,

*266 SHRI SURESH PACHOURI: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to State: 
(a) the present status of infant and maternal morbidity and mortality rate; 
(b) how this differs from State to State; 
(c) the factors responsible for high rate  of infant and maternal morbidity 
and mortality; 
(d) whether any targets have been fixed for reducing them; 
(e) if so, the details thereof; 
(f) how these have been achieved; and 
(g) the steps taken by Government to tackle the problem? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI 
SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) to (g) A Statement is laid on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
As per Sample Registration System (S RS) of Registrar General of India, 
the latest available Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) for India for the year 2001 
(provisional) is 66 per thousand live births. The IMR has declined from 68 in 
2000 to 66 in 2001. The IMRs for all the States for 
20 

[10 March, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
the year 2001 (provisional) are given in Statement-I (See below). The latest 
available Maternal Mortality Rate (MMR) for the year 1998 is 407 per 
1,00,000 live births. State-wise MMRs for 1998 for bigger States are given in 
Statement-ll (See below). The MMR for the subsequent years have not be 
compiled by Registrar General of India due to inadequate sample size. 
The major reasons for high infant mortality continue to be poor nutrition, 
inadequate maternal and newborn care and acute respiratory infections, 
diarrhoeal diseases and vaccine preventable diseases (in places where 
immunization coverage has not reached optimum levels). The main causes of 
maternal mortality are haemorrhage, complications during delivary, anaemia, 
abortion related, pregnancy induced hypertension, obstructed labour and 
others. Low socio-economic status of women, low level of female education 
and lack of access to health services are also the contributing factors for high 
IMR and MMR. 
Government of India has formulated the National Population Policy, 2000 
which envisages a policy framework for advancing goals and prioritizing 
strategies to meet the Reproductive and Child Health needs. This Policy aims at 
reduction of IMR to less than 30 per thousand live births and MMR to 100 per 
lakh live births by 2010. The Tenth Five Year Plan envisages reduction of IMR 
to 45 per thousand live births and MMR to 200 per 1,00,000 live births by the 
year 2007. 
The focus of Reproductive and Child Health Programme is to provide need-
based, demand-driven, client-oriented, integrated delivery of services at sub-
centre, PHC and CHC level through decentralized participatory planning. The 
interventions are beign carried out through a vast network of primary health care 
system through 1,37,271 sub centers, 22,975 primary health centers, 2,935 
community health centers and 1,748 First Referral Units. Besides, there are 
district hospitals, general hospitals and teachning hospitals that provide 
secondary and tertiary level care. In add ition to the above, in order to further 
improve the outreach services, schemes have also been initiated viz. 
Reproductive and Child Health camps, RCH Outreach Schemes, Dai Training 
Programme etc. 
Under the Reproductive and Child Health Programme, interventions for 
reduction in child mortality and morbidity are beign implemented in all 
districts of the country. Interventions for children include immunization against 
six vaccine preventable diseases; control of deaths due to 
21 

RAJYA SABHA [10 March, 2003] 
Diarrhoea; control of Acute Respiratory Infections; Prophylaxis against 
Vitamin A deficiency; and Iron deficiency anaemia; Essetinal Newborn Care; 
Promotion of exclusive Breastfeeding and appropriate complementary feeding 
practices. 
For mothers, the interventions include essential obstetric care; emergency 
obstetric care; provision of referral transport through Panchayats and provision 
of durgs and equipment of first referral units; provision of contractual staff like 
additional Auxiliary Nurse Midwives (ANMs), staff nurses, doctors and 
anesthetists. Funds are also being provided for schemes to improve outreach 
of services like 24 hours delivery services in selected primary health centers 
and community health centers; improvement of safe deliveries through trained 
Dais in every village, holding of Reportoductive and Child Health camps in 
178 districts and RCH Outreach Scheme in 151 districts with adverse health 
indicators,

RAJYA SABHA [10 March, 2003] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF INFORMATION 
AND BROADCASTING (SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD): (a) Under 
the provisions of Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995, cable 
operators are required to register themselves with the Head Post Master of 
their areas of operation. There is no restriction on the number of cable 
operators operating in an area, provided the applicant fulfils the prescribed 
eligibility conditions. 
(b) to (e) The subscription fees charged by the cable operators is, at 
present, a commercial arrangement between the subscribers, cable operators 
and Broadcasters. Hitherto there was no provision to regulate the subscription 
charges under Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995. The 
Ministry had received a number of complaints about the frequent and 
arbitrary hike in subscription rates and lack of transparency in the cable 
distribution system. The Act of 1995 was therefore, amended through Cable 
Television Networks (Regulation) Amendment Act, 2002 under which the 
Central Government has the power to specify the maximum amount, which a 
cable operator may demand from the subscribers for the programmes 
transmitted in the basic service tier of free to air channels. However, there is 
no provision to regulate the charge for pay channels, which would be 
transmitted only through an addressable system. 
In exercise of the powers conferred by Sub-section (1) of Section 4A of 
Gable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995, the Central Government 
by Notification dated 14.1.2003 has notified the 15th January, 2003 as the 
date within six months from which, it shall be obligatory for every cable 
operator to transmit/retransmit programmes of any pay channel through an 
addressable system, in four metro cities of Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai. 
Thereafter a set top box will be required  at the consumers' premises to view 
the pay channels, but not for viewing the free to air channels. The consumer 
will benefit, because he can choose and pay only for the channels, which he 
wishes to watch. A Task Force has been constituted to examine various issues 
related to implementation of CAS. The focus of its deliberations will be on 
protection of consumer interest.

Revamping the tea auction system 
1856. SHRI SURENDRA LATH: Will the Minister of COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the growing variation in the prices 
of tea in the domestic market as well as in the field of export; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether there is a need to revamp the tea auction system to bolster 
tea prices; and 
(d) the other steps being taken to resolve the problems in the tea 
industry? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI ARUN 
JAITLEY): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The au ction prices of tea in the domestic 
market have fluctuated over the years showing an overall decline since 1999. 
The decline in domestic price of tea is largely due to the oversupply of tea in the 
international market, low demand from domestic and export sectors and quality 
considerations. The unit export price realisation of tea has also shown a decline 
being dependant upon the prevailing primary prices (at the domestic auctions and 
in private sale from the producer), the international prices of the different 
grades, and specificallly the CIF prices of competitive grades by competing 
countries in a specific market. Since about 24% of India teas are exported, the 
availability of teas of similar grades from other competing countries at a 
lower price tends to bring down the unit cost realisation. The decline in value

Impact of campaign on HIV 
1879. SHRI R.R GOENKA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have made any study about the impact of its 
campaign on the spread of HIV; 
(b) whether the campaign has resulted in safer behaviour; 
(c) the results of intervention programmes among sex workers; and 
(d) whether the HIV epidemic would come under control in the near 
future? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE 
(SHRIMATI SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. A nationwide baseline 
Behavioural Surveillance Survey was conducted by the National AIDS 
Control Organisation in the year 2001 and 2002 among general population 
and high risk group in the age group 15-49 years. The study revealed that 
71.2% of the respondents stated that HIV/AIDS can be prevented by sexual 
abstinence and 57% stated that HIV/AIDS can be prevented by having one 
faithful uninfected sexual partner. The study also revealed that 32.4% of 
respondents reported consistent condom use, with their non-regular sex 
partners in the last 12 months. 
The study also revealed that 93.5% of sex workers had heard of 
HIV/AIDS and 82.7% were aware about protection from HIV/AIDS through 
consistent condom use. 76% of the sex workers reported condom use during 
the last sexual encounter with their paying clients. 
(d) The National AIDS Control Organisation has been conducting 
nationwide sentinel surveillance every year since 1998 to track the trends of 
HIV spread in the country. The data obtained from the sentinel, surveillance is 
also used for estimation of the total number of HIV infections. The estimated 
number of HIV infections was 3.5 million in the year 1998, 3.71 million in 
1999, 3.86 million in 2000 and 3.97 million in 2001 .These estimates indicate 
that there is no upsurge in the spread of HIV infection in the country.

regularly to create public awareness through Radio, Television, newspaper,

AIDS vaccine by American Pharmaceuticals Company 
1909. SHRIMATI SHABANA AZMI: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether according to the US Central Intelligence Agency, India is fast 
approaching dangerous levels of HIV infection with upto 25 million HIV 
positive cases more than any other country-projected for the year 2010; 
(b) if so, whether an American Pharmaceuticals Company claimed to be 
in final state of testing an AIDS vaccine; 
(c) whether a legislation to safeguard human rights of those infected by 
HIV/AIDS is being considered by Government following recommendations 
of International Policy-makers Conference; and 
(d) if so, the concrete programme of action to tackle AIDS considered by 
Government? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE 
(SHRIMATI SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) It is claimed in a recent report of the 
National Intelligence Council in the USA that "approximately 20-25 million 
Indians are likely to be infected (with HIV) by 2010". 
(b) Yes, Sir. An American pharmaceutical company, Vaxgen has 
completed phase III clinical trials for the "AIDS VAX" vaccine, which is a gp 
120 sub-unit HIV 1 sub-type B vaccine.The results are not perceived as 
encouraging, and the detailed analysis shows very limited success. 
(c) An International Policy Makers Conference on HIV/AIDS was held 
at New Delhi on May 10-12-2002. One of the key issues discussed at the 
conference was the need for comprehensive legislative measures to combat 
HIV/AIDS and its impact in the society. A Delhi declaration adopted at the 
end of the conference pledged to "Strengthen legislative and regualtory 
systems and procedures" to fight the epidemic. As a follow up of the Delhi 
declaration a special legislative group was constituted at the time, to examine 
existing legislations and ways to develop a comprehensive legislation to 
safeguard the rights of the people living with HIV/AIDS and other vulnerable 
populations. 
(d) In order to prevent and control the spread of HIV/AIDS in India, 
Govt, of India has launched a comprehensive National AIDS Control 
109 

RAJYA SABHA [10 March, 2003] 
Programme, currently under implementation throughout the country as a 
centrally sponsored scheme with the following components:— 
* Preventive interventions for high risk populations through 
targeted interventions adopting a multi-pronged strategy 
including peer counseling and behaviour change communication. 
* Preventive interventions for the general population through 
programmes for blood safety, voluntry counseling and testing 
services, information education and communication (IEC) and 
awareness building among adolescents and sensitization for the 
AIDS Vaccine Initiative. 
* Provision of low cost care and support services by providing 
community care services, treatment of opportunistic infections and 
prevention of occupational exposure. 
* Collaborative efforts to promote inter-sectoral programme 
activities including workplace interventions and public-private 
partnerships. 
* Build technical and managerial capacities for programme 
implementation through Surveillance, Training, Monitoring and 
Evaluation, Technical resource groups, operational research and 
Programme management. 
Mustard Oil 
1910. SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE: Will the Minister of 
HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that recent research has revealed that the mustard 
oil has been found to be the most superior edible oil to all other cooking 
medium and is the cure-all for life-style illness; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether there is any proposal to carry out any special campaign to 
create awareness among the people in order to make them health conscious; 
and 
(d) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
110 

[10 March, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE 
(SHRIMATI SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) to (d) According to Indian Council of 
Medical Research, no single oil is either most superior to all other cooking 
media or can it be a cure for all life style illness. Lifestyle illnesses are due to 
multiple factors including faulty dietary habits. One of the dietary components 
which affects these disease is the quantity and type of edible oil consumed. 
Edible oil contains various proportions of fatty acids. To derive the maximum 
nutritional and health benefits of alpha-linoleic acid (n-3) present in 
mustard/rapeseed oil and reduce erucic acid intake, the Indian Council of 
Medical Research's National Institute of Nutrition, Hyderabad has 
recommended the use of mustard oil along with any other vegetable oil of 
choice. 
National Institute of Nutrition under the Indian Council of Medical 
Research from time to time issue books/pamphlets and simple messages for 
creating awareness among the people in order to make them health conscious.

women is not available. However, as per the Sample Registration System of the 
Registrar General of India, the Material Mortality Ratio of India was 407 in 
1998. Based on this data on Maternal Mortality Ratio, it is estimated that about 
1.1 lakh women die every year due to causes related to pregnancy and child 
birth. 
The main causes of maternal deaths are:— 
1. Direct Causes: Hemorrhage, infections, Obstructed Labor, 
Unsafe Abortion, Toxemia or Pregnancy etc. 
2. Indirect Causes: Anemia, Viral Hepatitis, Tuberculosis and 
Malaria. 
3. Socio economic causes: Early age of marriage adolescent 
pregnancy, low status of women, low level of femal education, lack 
of access to health services, gender bias and economic 
dependency. 
(b) and (c) Maternal Health  is an integral part of the Reproductive and 
Child Health Programme which aims at bringing down the maternal mortality 
and morbidity. Under this programme various interventions focused on 
reducing maternal deaths are being implemented. These are essential obstetric 
care; Emergency Obstetric Care; provision for referral transport for pregnant 
women with complication of pregnancy through panchayats; provision of 
drugs and equipment at first referral units; provision of contractual staff like 
additional health workers, staff nurses, doctors and anesthetists. Funds are 
also being provided for schemes like 24 hours delivery services at selected 
primary health centres and community health centres. 
In order to improve safe deliveries, a Dai training Programme is 
currently being undertaken in 166 districts in 19 States. For making services 
available in remote, inaccessible and underutilized PHCs, a scheme of 
holding Reproductive and Child Health camps is being implemented in 172 
districts in 28 States/UTs and outreach strengthening project in 151 districts. 
Funds are also being provided to the districts under the National Maternity 
Benefit Scheme, wherein pregnant women belonging to families below the 
poverty line get Rs. 500/- for the first two live births. 
The need for bringing down MMR considerably and improving maternal 
health in general has been strongly stressed in the National

brining about total inter-sectoral coordination at the grassroots level and also

Statement 
Guidelines for Applying Licenses for Setting up Community 
Radio Station 
PREAMBLE 
The Union Government has decided to grant Community Broadcasting 
licenses to well established educational institutions/ organizations recognized 
by the Central Government or the State Government. These will include the 
Universities and institutes of Technology/Management and residential school. 
The salient features of eligibility criteria, basic conditions/obligations and 
procedures for obtaining license to set up and operate Community Radio 
service are briefly described below:- For further details reference may be made 
to Ministry of Information & Broadcasting. 
2. Technical parameters: 
2.1 Licence will be granted for FM transmitters for power of 50 Watts or 
less. 
2.2 Licence will be issued in the shared frequency band from 87.5 
145 

RAJYA SABHA [10 March, 2003] 
to 100 Mhz. However, in the event of frequency not being available in this 
band, the exclusive broadcast band of 104 to 108 Mhz may also be considered, 
as in case of private FM broadcasters. The frequency band from 100 to 104 
Mhz earmarked exclusively for the use of AIR, Prasar Bharati will not be 
disturbed. 
3. Procedure to be followed: 
Application:— 
3.1 Any eligible institution/organization desirous of setting up of 
Community Radio broadcasting service may make an application to the 
Ministry of l&B in the prescribed proforma. (Download application form). 
13.2 The Ministry of l&B immediately on reciept of an application will 
consult the Wireless Advisor in WPC wing of Ministry of Communications and 
also Prasar Bharati to determine the availability of frequency at the place 
requested by the applicant. 
3.3 The Ministry of Information & Broadcasting will refere the eligible 
applicant case to the Ministries of Home Affairs, Defence, Human Resources 
Development and External Affairs and letter of intent and/or license will be 
issued only after getting the requisite clearances from these Ministries. The 
licensee will be required to sign a licence agreement after allotment of frequency 
by WPC. The license agreement shall specify detailed terms and conditions under 
which the licence is to be operated. 
3.4 Within one year from the date of signing of licence agreement, the 
applicant will complete all necessary formalities such as obtaining SACFA 
clearance etc., set up the necessary broadcast facilities and obtain a Wireless 
Operating Licence from the Wireless Advisor in the WPC Wing of the 
Ministry of Communications and Information Technology. 
3.5 In the event of more than one claimant for a single frequency at a 
given place, the licensee will be selected by a Committee constituted by the 
Ministry of l&B on the basis of standing, commitment, objectives and 
resources of the applicant organization. 
3.6 Licensee will be charged only the spectrum usage fee as 
determined by the WPC. The Ministry of l&B will rtot levy and other licence 
fee. 
146 

[10 March, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
4. Terms and Conditions 
4.1 The basic objective of the Community Radio broadcasting would be to 
serve the cause of the community in the service area of the licensee by involving 
members of the community in the broadcasting of their programmes. For this 
purpose community would mean people living in the coverage zone of the 
broadcasting service of the licensee. 
4.2 The licence shall be for a period of three (3) years. 
4.3 The licence shall not be transferable. 
4.4 An applicant will not be permitted more than one licence. 
4.5 The licensee shall provide its services on free to air basis. 
4.6 The licensee shall not use its channel/broadcast services in whole or part 
for commercial purposes. 
4.7 The programmes on the community radio service will focus on issues 
relating to education, health, environment, agriculture rural and community 
development. The content must be confined to social, cultural and local issues 
and the format, subject, presentation and language must reflect and exude the 
local flavour and fragrance. 
4.8 The licensee shall not be permitted to broadcast any news and current 
affairs programmes and shall not air election and political broadcasts. 
4.9 The licensee shall not air any advertisement or sponsored 
programmes. 
4.10 The licensee shall ensure that nothing is included in the 
programme of the licensee which: 
a. Offends against good taste or decency; 
b. Contains criticism of friendly countries; 
c. Contains attack on religious or communities or visuals or 
words contemptuous of religious groups or which promote 
communal attitudes; 
d. Contains anything obscene, defamatory, deliberate, false and 
suggestive innuendos and half truths; 
e. Is likely to encourage or incite violence or contains anything 
against maintenance of law and order ot which promote-anti- 
national attitudes; 
147 

RAJYA SABHA [10 March, 2003] 
f. Contains anyining amounting to contempt of court; 
g. Contains aspersions against the integrity of the President and 
Judiciary; 
h. Contains anything affecting the integrity of the Nation; 
i. Criticises, maligns or slanders any individual in person or certain 
groups, segments of social public and moral life of the country; 
j. Encourages superstition or blind belief; 
k. Denigrates women; 
I. Denigrates children. 
m. May presem/depict/suggesi as desirable the misuse of drugs 
including alcohol, narcotics and tobacco or which may stereotype, 
incite, vilify or perpetuate hatred against or attempt to demean any 
person or group on the basis of ethnicity, nationality, race, gender, 
sexual preference, religion, age or physical or mental disability. 
4.11 The licensee shall ensure that due care is taken with respect to 
religious programmes with a view to avoiding:— 
a) improper exploitation of religious susceptibilities; and 
d) offence to the religious views and beliefs of those belonging to a 
particular religion or religious denomination. 
4.12 That the licensee shall ensure that due emphasis is given in the 
programmes to promote values of national integration, religious harmony, 
scientific temper and Indian culture. 
4.13 The licensee shall follow the Programme Code of All India Radio. 
4.14 The licensee shall pay spectrum usage fee as determined by the 
Wireless Advisor in WPC Wing. 
4.15 Though the licensees will operate the service under the Ministry of 
Information & Broadcasting, Govt, of India, the licensing will be subject to the 
condition that as and when any regulatory authority to regulate and monitor 
the broadcast services in the country is constituted, the licensees will have fo 
adhere to the norms, rules and regulations prescribed by such authority. 
148 

[10 March, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
4.16 The licensee shall provide such information to the Government on such 
intervals as may be required. In this connection, the licensee is required to preserve 
tapes of programmes broadcast during the last six months failing which the 
Government will be at liberty to revoke the license. 
4.17 The Government or its authorized representative shall have the right to 
inspect the broadcast facilities of the licensees and collect such information as 
considered necessary in public and community interests. 
4.18 The Government reserves the right to take over the entire services and 
networks of the licensee or revoke/terminate/suspend the licence in the interest of 
national security or in the event of national emergency/war or low intensity conflict 
or similar type of situations. 
4.19 All foreign personnel likely to be deployed by way of appointment, contract, 
consultancy, etc. by the licensee for installation, maintenance and operation of the 
licensee's services shall be required to obtain security clearance from the 
Government of India. 
4.20 The Government reserves tht right to modify at any time the terms and 
conditions if it is necessary to do so in the interest of the general public or for the 
proper conduct of broadcasting or for security considerations. 
4.21 Government may revoke the licence at any time in public interest or for breach 
of any terms and conditions of the licence by giving a notice of 15 days. 
4.22 Notwithstanding anything contained anywhere else in the licence the 
Government's decision shall be final and conclusive. 
 
4.23 The licensees shall furnish a bank guarantee for a sum of Rs. 50,000/- 
(Rupees fifty thousand) only to ensure timely performance of the licence 
agreement. 
4.24 If the licensee fail to commission services within the stipulated period, he 
shall forfeit the amount of bank guarantee to the Government and the Government 
would be free to cancel the licence awarded to the licensee. 
4.25 A license will be subject to such other conditions as may be determined 
by the Government.

Study on the working of the Anti-defection Law 
1957. SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: Will the Minister of LAW 
AND JUSTICE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have carried out any study on the working of the 
Anti-defection Law which was put in place in 1985 through an amendment of 
the Constitution by adding Tenth Schedule thereto; and 
(b) if so, the details of the study so made? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JU STICE (SHRI ARUN JAITLEY): 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(1) Recommendation of Dinesh Goswami Committee:— 
(i) Provisions for disqualification should be limited to cases of (a) 
voluntarily giving up by an elected member of his membership of 
the political party to which the member belongs; and (b) voting or 
absention from voting by a member contrary to his party's 
directions or whip only in respect of a motion of vote of 
confidence or a motion amounting to no confidence or Money 
Bill or motion of vote of thanks to the President's Address. 
Further, the Deputy Speaker of the House of the People or the 
Legislative Assembly of a State, the Deputy Chairman of Council 
of States or Legislative Council of a State or a person occupying 
the Chair for the time being in the absence of any elected 
Presiding Officer, as the case may be, should not incur 
disqualification if he chooses to abstain from voting contrary to 
his party's directions or whip. 
(ii) The power of deciding the legal issue of disqualification should 
not be left to the Speaker or Chairman of the House but to the 
President or the Governor, as the case may be, who shall act on 
the advice of the Election Commission, to whom the question 
whould be referred fo r determination as in the case of any other 
post-election disqualification of a member; 
159 

RAJYA SABHA [10 March, 2003] 
(iii) A nominated member of the House should incur disqualification if 
he joins any political party at any period of time. 
(2) Suggestbns emanating from Judgement of the Supreme Court:— 
(i) The Supreme Court in the case of Kihota Hollohon Vs Zachilhu and 
others, [1992(1) SCALE 338-364(4)] by a majority judgement 
upheld the validity of the Tenth Schedule to the Constitution of 
India except paragraph 7 thereof. Paragraph 7 barred jurisdiction 
of courts in respect of any matter connected with disqualification 
of a member of House under the Tenth Schedule. The implication 
of the judgement is that the decisions of the Presiding Officer couid 
be scrutinised by the Courts on tne ground that in deciding the 
issues of defection, they were acting as tribunals. 
(ii) Pursuant to aforesaid judgment of the Supreme Court, a suggestion 
was made in a conference of the Presiding Officers of various State 
Legislatures which was presided over by the Speaker held in 1992 
that a privision may be made in the Anti-defection Law to provide 
for an appellate authority which would hear appeals from the 
judgment of the Presiding Officers so that decisions of the 
Presiding Officer were not directly scrutinised by the Courts. 
(iii) Pursuant fo the aforesaid suggestion, one of the proposals 
regarding constitution of an appellate authority was that in case 
of Members of Parliament, such authority may be President of 
India who shall obtain opinion of a Committee consisting of three 
members indicated in section 3(2) of the Judges Inquiries Act, 
1968, namely, a Judge of the Supreme Court, Chief Justice of a 
High Court and a distinguished jurist and shall act according to such 
opinion. Similar provision was proposed for Members of State 
Legislatures. 
(3) Recommendations of the Election Commission of India.— 
Anti-defection law may be amended leaving it to the President and 
the Governors concerned to decide cases of disqualification under 
the Tenth Schedule, after obtaining the opinion of the Election 
Commission. 
160 

[10 March, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
(4) Recommendations of the Law Commission in its 170th Report:— 
(i) Omission of definition of legislature party. 
(ii) New definition of political party to include pre-election fronts and 
coalitions for the purpose of Tenth Schedule. 
(iii) Doing away with the concept of split and merger. 
(iv) The question of disqualification for membership of Lok Sabha/ State 
Legislative Assemblies, after election be entrusted to the 
President/Governor for decision. 
(5) Recommendation of the National Commission to Review the 
Working of the Constitution:—  
The Provision of the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution should be 
amended specifically to provide that all persons defecting—
whether individually or in groups—from the party or the alliance 
of parties, on whose ticket they had been elected, must resign 
from their Parliamentary or Assembly seats and must contest 
fresh elections. In other words such persons should lose their 
membership and the protection under the provision of split etc. 
should be scrapped. The defectors should also be debarred from 
holding any public office as Ministers or any other remunerative 
political post for at least the duration of the remaining term of the 
existing Legislature of unitl, the next fresh elections whichever is 
earlier. The vote cast by a defector to topple a Government 
should be treated as invalid. Further, the power to decide question 
regarding disqualification on ground of defection should vest in 
the Election Commission instead of the Chairman or Speaker of 
the House concerned.

National Slum Development Policy 
1994. SHRI M.V. RAJASEKHARAN: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government are planning to bring National Slum 
Development Policy; 
(b) if so, whether any comprehensive study has been done so far, to 
identify the number of slums and affected people in the Country; and 
(c) if so, whether any comprehensive plan is being considered for 
developing all the slums in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI PON 
RADHAKRISHNAN): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Slum development being a State subject, State Governments 
survey and taken stock of slums in their respective States. However, the 
Town and Country Planning Organization (TCPO) conducted a one-time 
study on slums in 1995-96 and brought out a report titled "A Compendium 
on Indian Slums-1996." 
An attempt has been made for the first time during the Census of India, 
2001 by the Registrar General of India to collect detailed data about slum areas of 
the country particularly in cities/towns having 50,000 population or more 
based on 1991 census. As per the provisional figures of Census of India, 2001 the 
number of towns reporting slums is 607 and the total provisional slum population 
of these towns is reported at 402.97 lakhs. 
(c) Slum Deveiopoment is a State subject. The State Governments 
formulate specific plans, programmes and schemes for development of 
slums in various cities as per their priorities and make necessary 
provisions therefor, in their respective State Plans. To improve the living 
standards of slum dwellers Dy providing the basic facilities, Environmental 
Improvement of Urban slums (EIUS) is being implemented in the State 
Sector. Besides, National Slum Development Programme (NSDP) was 
189 

RAJYA SABHA [10 March, 2003] 
launched by the Central Government in August, 1996 to ameliorate the living 
conditions of slum dwellers. Under this Programme Additional Central 
Assistance (ACA) is being provided to theStates/UTs for provision of basic 
amenities. 
In 2001, Valmiki Ambedkar Awas Yojana (VAMBAY) was launched to 
provide shelter or upgrade the existing shelter for people living below the 
poverty line in urban slums. There is also a component for providing 
community toilets under Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan.

Eco-Environmehtal Threat to Chiika Lake, Orissa 
DR. M.N. DAS (Orissa) : Madam, the Chiika lake, which is the largest 
lake of Asia, covering 110 square kilometres of water space in southern 
Orissa, is famous not only for its natural beauty but also for its ecological 
wonders.   Rich with marine life and marine wealth, it presents a 
211 

RAJYA SABHA            [10 March, 2003] 
rare phenomenon when hundreds of, thousands of migratory birds from colder 
regions in far away north, including Siberia fly over unknown distances to 
spend winter months at the Chilka Lake. These migratory birds belong to 
numerous species and thousands of them are regarded as rarest of the rare. 
Ecologists and environmentalists from several countries come over here to 
study these rare birds every winter. Such a wonder lake is recently threatened 
both by nature and men, and is facing challenges to its natural existence. 
Nature plays havoc by silting up its mouth to sea and reducing its salinity 
index, which adversely affects both aquatic vegetation and marine life. Men 
come forward to make money by prawn cultivation and encroaching upon 
water space of the lake. These men possess physical and money power. They 
resort to reckless fishing during breeding season and reduce timely growth of 
marine resources. Much more dangerous than all these activities is the latest 
invasion by poachers who kill large number of migratory birds Dy various 
means, to eat their flesh and to earn money by exporting dead birds. Unless 
the Department of Environment of the Union Government and various 
concerned agencies of the State Government of Orissa jointly intervene to 
take strong measures against invaders of the Chilka Lake, this most beautiful 
lake of India will lose its charm and its value. Mouth-siltation should also be 
prevented. Thank you.

THE CUSTOMS TARIFF (AMENDMENT) BILL, 2003 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI GINGEE N. RAMACHANDRAN) : Madam, I beg 
to move: 
"That the Bill further to amend the Customs Tariff Act, 1975, as 
passed by Lok Sabha, be taken into consideration." 
Madam, due to the urgency for replacing the Customs Tariff (Amendment) 
Ordinance, we have introduced the Customs Tariff (Amendment) Bill, 2003, 
that is already passed by the Lok Sabha on the 3 rd March, this year. It is sent 
to this House for consideration. For having a uniformity in the Government 
classification codes prevailing for customs tariff purposes and also for 
commercial purposes, which are adopted by the Commerce Department, and 
also by the international organisations,-to expand the six-digit classification 
code to the eight-digit classification code, we have introduced this Bill. It seeks 
to replace the Customs Tariff (Amendment) Ordinance, 2003 also. Now, the 
customs tariff is classified under the six-digit code. The Commerce 
Department has adopted 8-digit code in order to harmonise the commodities 
in one code which will reduce the transit cost and other classifications and 
disputes. For that reason, we have introduced this Bill to replace the 
Ordinance. On that matter, it has already been taken up in the Lok Sabha. It 
has come up for discussion in the Rajya Sabha. After hearing all your points, I 
will give my reply. 
The question was proposed. 
SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE (West Bengal) : Madam, I rise to make 
my observations on this Bill. The Bill, as you know, is one of the bulkiest 
documents, containing 554 pages. But all the pages contain the  schedules 
and a large number of items. The whole objective of my participation in this 
Bill is just to travel back in the memory lane, in the sense that 28 years ago, 
sitting on that side, I had the privilege of piloting the Bill now the principal Act, 
the Customs Tariff Act, 1975, which was based on the harmonised system of 
nomenclature, which was popularly known as BTN, Brussels Tariff 
Nomenclature, it was evolved by the Customs World Organisation located at 
Brussels. At that point of time this harmonised system was based on 6 digits. 
Now, the Department of Revenue  has  evolved  over  the  years  a  system  
of  8  digits.     Certain 
219 

      RAJYA SABHA              [10 March. 2003] 
organisations have evolved 10 digits system. Already, from the 1 st of April, 
2002, the 8-digit harmonised system of nomenclature have been introduced. 
Now, two questions arise, and, if the movers of the Statutory Resolution were 
there, they could have pointed it out as to why it has been brought in the form 
of an Ordinance, because the Government wanted to introduce the 8-digit 
harmonised system of nomenclature, recommended by the Customs World 
Trade Organisation. No harm, everybody accepts that and it should be done. It 
was introduced from 1" April, 2002. Therefore, in the July Session, in the 
Monsoon Session, we could have got it done through the regular legislation. In 
Winter Session also, we could have done it. There was no need of bringing it 
in the form of Ordinance in the month of January. I object to the principle of 
making financial legislations. It is a money Bill as defined under Article 110. 
Financial legislations need not necessarily be routed through the ordinance 
route; it should be done through regular legislations. Secondly, when, for the 
last 10 years, we have evolved a system of scrutinising the important pieces of 
legislation by the Standing Committees, there would have been no harm if this 
Bill would have passed through the scrutiny of the appropriate Standing 
Committee, in this case the Standing Committee of the Finance Ministry. I am 
repeating the point. The code has been evolved by the Department of 
Revenue. There have been consultations with the DGFT, Director-General of 
Foreign Trade. The Director-General of Commercial Intelligence and Statistics 
has been consulted. Various Chambers of Commerce, representatives of the 
trade and industry have also  given their inputs, and if the Members of this 
Standing Committee, dealing with money and finance, could have given their 
inputs, I think, the Bill would have become better, from the presentation point 
of view and from the appreciation point of view. There was no urgency as such 
that a legislation through the Ordinance route should have taken place. But

SHRI GINGEE N. RAMACHANDRAN : Madam, this Bill replacing the 
Customs Tariff (Amendment) Ordinance, 2003, has already been passed by 
the Lok Sabha. The Ordinance was promulgated in the month of January due 
to certain exigencies. The hon. Member, Shri Pranab Mukherjee, asked, 
instead of coming to Parliament, what was the emergency that necessitated 
the promulgation of this Ordinance. I want to clarify this point. 
The Customs Tariff (Amendment) Ordinance, 2003 was promulgated 
for bringing tariffs under one common code. We had adopted a six digit 
classification code. The Commerce Ministry has an eight digit classification 
code, which is followed by the Commerce Ministry. We have adopted that 
code to facilitate trade and industry, based on customs departments eight digit 
classification code. It is for that purpose that we have adopted it. After taking 
into careful consideration the classification codes adopted by the Commerce 
Ministry and others, we have adopted this common code. Internationally also, 
there are many countries which have adopted a ten digit classification code, 
an eight digit classification code, a six digit classification 
228 

[10 March, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
code and so on. The Department of Revenue, the Director General of Foreign 
Trade and the Director General of Commercial Intelligence and Statistics and 
Sales Tax Department of various State Governments and the Central 
Statistics Organisation have been consulted on the Common Classification 
Code. I would like to inform the House that if there is any difference between 
the Department of Revenue and the Department of Commerce, then it would 
lead to litigation. It will take more time to know about the actual quantum that 
we have imported, what the actual tariff duty is. For these reasons, we have 
brought forward this legislation. This legislation also has been brought forward 
in order to reduce the transition costs. We have brought forward this 
legislation through an Ordinance, and now we are replacing it with this Bill. 
I would like to inform the hon. Members that we are going to pass the 
Finance Bill. Before passing the Finance ~ Bill, if we promulgate the Ordnance 
regarding the Customs Common Code, which is harmonised with 
nomenclature, it will be followed by the Finance Bill, only then the Finance Bill 
will be able to accommodate whatever has been stipulated in the Code. At the 
same time, the Commerce Ministry has also adopted the Exim Policy which 
will be effective from irt April, 2003. For these two reasons, we wanted that the 
Ordinance should be promulgated well in advance, before introducing the 
Finance Bill and before taking into consideration the Exim Policy. Now, I am 
replacing that Ordinance with this Bill. 
Hon. Members expressed various concerns about the WTO. We are 
a signatory to the WTO. We have come to an understanding to bring a two-tier 
system, but we are having power to raise custom duty to protect our 
industries. The hon. Member has already made a mention of that. The 
introduction of Common Classification Code will give more flexibility to various 
categories. Suppose, one item is classified under one head, if there are sub-
heads, then we will have more. Now, instead of six digits, we will have eight 
digits. It will give us more scope for flexibility. We can take our own decisions 
because we have to protect the interests of our local industries. This process 
is going on in the WTO negotiations. For this reason also, we had to 
promulgate this Ordinance. 
Madam, I want to bring this matter to the attention of the hon. 
Members of this House that this will facilitate trade and commerce; it will 
reduce the transition costs; the importers would be able to import easily and

Magistrate and immediately the money was refunded. No further action was 
required to be taken because the money was refunded. 
There are two other examples; one in Andhra Pradesh and the other 
In West Bengal, where the Members of Parliament complained that - it was also 
published in the newspapers - the party is dictating as to what should be done 
with the MPLADS funds. So long as the schemes are concerned, if they 
adhere to the guidelines, we cannot enquire into the matter. But, so far as 
these particular complaints of the MPs are concerned, we cannot look into the 
matter unless there is a complaint lodged with us. 
So, I was submitting, that the position as of today is that the 
percentage of utilisation of funds has gone up. In the year 1998, this figure was 
54 per cent. In the year 1999, this figure was 63 per cent. Subsequently, in the 
year 2000, it went to 64 per cent and in the year 2001, it reached 65 per cent. 
This figure went upto 74 per cent in the year 2002 and 78.7 per cent in the year 
2003. This is the utilisation of the MPLADS funds. 
Now, Sir, as I said, if there is a specific charge levelled against a 
particular MP, it can be enquired into. We all know that the tape recording is 
not evidence by itself. It has to be corroborated. The newspaper publications 
are not evidence by themselves; it has to be corroborated. Merely because 
something has been said or has been shown in the videotapes; it does not 
mean that there is proof of the incident. Unless and until, there is a particular 
complaint or there is an evidence to show that this has happened, there is no 
question of inquiring into the matter. So far as this particular Ministry is 
concerned, as I have said, we must proceed on the basis of faith and 
confidence. We cannot say that all the MPs are doing this thing and that they 
are misappropriating funds. There is no evidence also.   We proceed on the 
assumption that they are honest and I 
328 

[10 March, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
have no doubt in my mind that they are honest and the MPs are doing their 
work properly. As and when a particular complaint comes, that can be 
inquired into.   But as of now, there has been no such complaint. 
As I was submitting, Sir, so far as the MPLADS is concerned, a lot of 
work has been done not only in Uttar Pradesh but also in other States. Even 
in my State a lot of work has been done. There is no question of stopping it 
now. 
Lastly, I am grateful to the hon. Members for giving these valuable 
suggestions. Certainly, we will look into the matter. But as I said earlier, we 
are not discussing here the question of corruption in the country. It is not skin-
deep. It may be going into our marrows. But that is not the subject-matter of 
discussion today. The subject-matter of discussion today is whether on the 
basis of this tape-record with regard to the MPLADS it can be said that there 
is misappropriation of funds by the MPs. I respectfully submit that that is not 
evidence enough. But certainly it may be inquired into provided a proper 
complaint comes to the Ministry. Thank you.
